title: The US is building the Smartest AI. China is running a different race | Luisa Rodriguez

### Update: since we recorded [[00:00:00]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/china-ai-race-chips-slowdown/?t=0)

**Luisa Rodriguez:** Four days after we filmed this episode, NVIDIA’s CEO Jensen Huang admitted to an affair with a woman US intelligence reportedly believes is a Chinese spy.

According to the _[New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/08/technology/nvidia-investigation-jensen-huang.html)_, US officials believe she was recruited to gather information and potentially push for NVIDIA’s best chips to be sold to China.

This news shows just how much China wants American chips. Here’s the episode.

### Everyone said China had caught up [[00:00:30]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/china-ai-race-chips-slowdown/?t=30)

In December 2024, all of the world’s [most advanced AI companies](https://epoch.ai/data-insights/us-vs-china-eci) were in the US. A month later, [DeepSeek, a Chinese company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DeepSeek) most people had never heard of, seemed to blow that apart by [releasing an AI model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12948) that rivalled the best ones in the US.

They claimed to have trained it for just $6 million. Meanwhile, American companies were spending tens of millions to train their models.

Marc Andreessen called it [AI’s Sputnik moment](https://fortune.com/2025/01/27/marc-andreessen-deepseek-sputnik-ai-markets/). NVIDIA [lost almost $600 billion](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/chinas-deepseek-sets-off-ai-071458375.html) in value in one day — the biggest one-day loss in US stock market history.

Suddenly, everyone was saying: China had caught up.

They were only half right. Almost two years later, its models are still about [six months behind](https://ifp.org/how-to-increase-americas-ai-lead-over-china/) the best American ones. Still, six months isn’t that long — especially when you consider that the US has roughly 16 times China’s [AI computing power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compute_(machine_learning)).

So how are [Chinese models this good](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/sihao-huang-china-ai-capabilities/#how-advanced-is-chinese-ai-001521)?

If you think the US [can’t slow AI down](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/ai-slowdown-why-how/) because China will catch up, this might change your mind. Because China _is_ keeping up. But it couldn’t do that without American help.

### Who’s building China’s AI? [[00:01:50]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/china-ai-race-chips-slowdown/?t=110)

To understand how, it helps to start with who’s actually building China’s AI.

There are two kinds of players: tech giants like [Alibaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alibaba_Group), [Tencent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tencent), and [ByteDance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ByteDance), the company behind TikTok; and a handful of startups, like DeepSeek and [Zhipu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z.ai).

These companies are inventive. DeepSeek’s model was revolutionary for squeezing more out of fewer chips.

They’re also talented. More than half of the world’s top AI researchers did their [undergraduate degrees in China](https://carnegieendowment.org/features/whos-ahead-in-the-global-ai-talent-race). And more and more of them are staying there to work.

And they do one big thing differently to US companies: most of them [open source their best models](https://www.uscc.gov/research/two-loops-how-chinas-open-ai-strategy-reinforces-its-industrial-dominance). [Anyone can download them](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_weights) and build on them for free, which has made Chinese models [popular everywhere](https://huggingface.co/blog/huggingface/state-of-os-hf-spring-2026) — including in the US.

But it’s [very hard to make money](https://epoch.ai/publications/how-do-chinese-ai-companies-make-money) that way. China’s six leading AI companies [collectively earn about 10%](https://rhg.com/research/examining-chinas-ai-financing/) of what OpenAI and Anthropic do.

And while they’re big at home, they’re still small next to the leading American companies. [ByteDance’s chatbot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doubao) has [about 380 million monthly users](https://epoch.ai/publications/how-do-chinese-ai-companies-make-money). ChatGPT has [more than twice as many](https://openai.com/index/scaling-ai-for-everyone/)_every week_. And they have [far less computing power](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/lennart-heim-compute-governance/#why-focus-on-compute-002143) to build with.

So China’s AI industry is inventive and talented, but also comparatively small, poor, and starved for chips. And yet, its best models are surprisingly good.

### How far behind is China? [[00:03:20]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/china-ai-race-chips-slowdown/?t=200)

Across dozens of AI tests, China’s best models score about as well as American models scored [six and a half months ago](https://ifp.org/how-to-increase-americas-ai-lead-over-china/#how-big-is-the-us-china-ai-capabilities-gap).

Earlier this year, Anthropic built [Claude Mythos](https://www.anthropic.com/glasswing), the first AI model to raise serious national security concerns. China is expected to have a model just as good within months. So whatever worries you have about the most powerful American AI today, expect it from China about six months later.

A lot of people, myself included, think we need to make sure these systems are safe before we build even more powerful ones — even if that means slowing down.

But others argue the US [can’t afford to slow down](https://www.fortune.com/2023/04/07/former-google-ceo-eric-schmidt-against-6-month-a-i-pause-elon-musk-benefit-china-chatgpt-openai), because China won’t. And if the US _did_ slow down and China didn’t, history’s most powerful technology could be built by [an authoritarian government](https://80000hours.org/problem-profiles/risks-of-stable-totalitarianism/).

The White House’s AI plan is literally called “[Winning the Race](https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Americas-AI-Action-Plan.pdf).” [David Sacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Sacks), Trump’s former AI czar, put the logic simply: the US is “[only six to nine months ahead](https://www.foxbusiness.com/media/ex-white-house-ai-czar-warns-us-could-lose-ai-race-china-washington-overregulates) of China. So really, every month counts.”

If every month counts, it’s worth understanding what’s causing this gap: what’s holding China back, and what’s letting it build such good models anyways.

### Why can’t China make its own chips? [[00:04:40]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/china-ai-race-chips-slowdown/?t=280)

Let’s start with what holds China back. A lot of it comes down to chips.

AI runs on lots of specialised computer chips. Companies need them to build better models, and then to run those models for millions of users. More chips means you can do more of both.

The best AI chips need two things China struggles to get.

First: [the machines that make them](https://80000hours.org/career-reviews/ai-hardware/). Only one company in the world builds the most advanced ones: [ASML, in the Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ASML_Holding). And since 2019, starting under the first Trump administration, [the US and Dutch governments](https://www.csis.org/analysis/true-impact-allied-export-controls-us-and-chinese-semiconductor-manufacturing-equipment) have blocked selling them to China. China can make _decent_ chips, [with less advanced machines](https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/semiconductors/china-stockpiled-343-immersion-duv-tools-for-advanced-chipmaking-report-claims-270-asml-scanners-can-produce-7nm-processors-without-sanctioned-euv-tools) — just not the best ones.

The second thing China struggles to get is memory. AI chips need a special kind of very fast memory, and China can’t make enough of it. And [since December 2024, US rules](https://www.bis.gov/press-release/commerce-strengthens-export-controls-restrict-chinas-capability-produce-advanced-semiconductors-military) have banned selling it to China too.

So even Huawei, China’s leading chip designer, only used Chinese-made memory in [about 16%](https://ifp.org/how-to-increase-americas-ai-lead-over-china/#domestic-production) of this year’s AI chips. The rest rely on stockpiles, smuggling, or slower substitutes.

Add it all up, and the US makes about 50 times as much AI computing power as China. That’s largely because of [American export controls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_New_Export_Controls_on_Advanced_Computing_and_Semiconductors_to_China).

After DeepSeek, plenty of people said the [export controls had failed](https://www.cnbc.com/2025/05/21/NVIDIA-ceo-jensen-huang-slams-us-chip-restrictions-as-a-failure.html), including NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang.

But [where they’re actually enforced](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/sihao-huang-china-ai-capabilities/#chinas-semiconductor-industry-005947), [they do hold China back](https://darioamodei.com/post/on-deepseek-and-export-controls). In fact, they’re one of the few things that have actually [bought the US time](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/luke-muehlhauser-ai-safety-grantmaking-founding/#are-chip-export-controls-good-for-safety-005017).

### So where do China’s chips come from? [[00:06:24]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/china-ai-race-chips-slowdown/?t=384)

And yet, China still has a lot of computing power. So where is it all coming from? Mostly, it’s coming from the US.

By the end of next year, about [two-thirds of Chinese AI computing power](https://ifp.org/how-to-increase-americas-ai-lead-over-china/#executive-summary) will come from American chips. They get them three ways.

Some are bought legally. [In January, the US approved sales](https://www.bis.gov/press-release/department-commerce-revises-license-review-policy-semiconductors-exported-china) of one of NVIDIA’s top chips, the H200, to China — though [Beijing told](https://fortune.com/2026/01/08/china-reportedly-tells-tech-firms-to-pause-NVIDIA-h200-orders/) its AI companies to hold off, to protect its _own_ chip industry.

Chinese firms still needed chips, though. So they found another route. This year, they bought [more than a million NVIDIA graphics cards](https://ifp.org/how-to-increase-americas-ai-lead-over-china/#legal-imports) — the kind that are normally used for gaming and design, which fall _just_ under the export rules’ limits — to use on AI.

Some chips are smuggled. In one case, smugglers [peeled the NVIDIA labels off](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/us-authorities-shut-down-major-china-linked-ai-tech-smuggling-network) top AI chips and replaced them with a made-up brand. Altogether, the smuggling network moved, or tried to move, at least $160 million worth of chips.

But here too, enforcement can help, if it’s done right. When Washington [threatened to restrict AI chip shipments](https://www.malaymail.com/news/malaysia/2025/07/14/malaysia-acts-to-avoid-us-sanctions-amid-escalating-global-ai-chip-war/183871) to Malaysia, Malaysia started requiring permits to export them. Chinese imports of servers from Malaysia and Singapore then [fell by about 80%](https://ifp.org/how-to-increase-americas-ai-lead-over-china/#smuggling).

But the biggest channel is renting. And if you see China as a threat, this one feels particularly ridiculous.

You don’t need physical access to AI chips to use them. You can rent time on them in a data centre anywhere in the world.

US rules prevent NVIDIA from selling its best chips to Chinese companies. But they _don’t_ stop Chinese companies from renting _those same chips_ in a [data centre abroad](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/helen-toner-ai-policy-washington-dc/#are-data-centres-in-the-uae-good-for-democracy-005241). So that’s what they do.

The Chinese AI company Tencent has [a deal to rent top chips](https://www.trendforce.com/news/2026/10/01/news-tencent-reportedly-signs-7b-deal-to-lease-100000-ai-chips-from-oracle-in-southeast-asia/) from the American company Oracle. ByteDance runs a cluster of NVIDIA’s best chips in Norway. But the majority of the computing power being rented sits in Southeast Asia, mostly Malaysia and Singapore.

Here’s what that looks like. In 2025, [four Chinese engineers flew from Beijing](https://www.tovima.com/wsj/chinese-ai-companies-dodge-u-s-chip-curbs-by-flying-suitcases-of-hard-drives-abroad/) to Malaysia, where they’d rented about 300 servers full of NVIDIA chips. Sending that much data over the internet could have taken months, so they carried it in suitcases, each packed with 15 hard drives of training data. The plan was to train their model in Malaysia, and then just fly back with it.

Meanwhile, American companies don’t have enough chips. Amazon runs one of the world’s biggest cloud businesses, and they say they won’t have enough computing power to meet customer demand [this year or next](https://fortune.com/2026/07/30/andy-jassy-amazon-capex-demand-aws-pga-tour/). So a chip that doesn’t go to China doesn’t go to waste. Someone else buys it — mostly American customers.

And this is where, for me, the race argument starts to fall apart. You’d expect the people making it to want these channels closed. Instead, some of its loudest voices have pushed to sell China more chips.

NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang has warned “China is [just nanoseconds behind](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/nvda-nvidia-ceo-jensen-huang-163040007.html) the US.”

He’s _also_ said export controls cost NVIDIA [its Chinese market](https://www.cnbc.com/2025/05/28/nvidia-ceo-hammers-chip-controls-that-effectively-closed-china-.html). His solution is to sell China more NVIDIA chips, to keep Chinese developers using American technology. But notice how neatly that fits his business.

David Sacks said every month counts. But as White House AI czar, [he pushed to loosen](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/02/26/congress-pushes-back-on-nvidia-white-house-with-chip-export-limits.html) restrictions on NVIDIA’s sales abroad. [The New York Times found](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/11/30/technology/david-sacks-white-house-profits.html) he held stakes in 449 AI-related companies while shaping AI policy.

Sacks says ethics officials signed off. But [his ethics waivers](https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/Memo-David-Sacks-3.5.2025-1.pdf) were issued by the White House’s own lawyers, a month after [Trump fired the head](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/trump-office-of-government-ethics-director/) of the government’s independent ethics office. Either way, I think the incentives are worth noticing.

### How do you copy an AI? [[00:10:35]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/china-ai-race-chips-slowdown/?t=635)

OK, but even _with_ all those chips, the numbers don’t add up.

On computing power alone, researchers estimate China should be [about 13 months behind](https://ifp.org/how-to-increase-americas-ai-lead-over-china/#how-much-do-chinese-companies-gain-from-adversarial-distillation). So what’s making up that difference?

The answer is something called “[distillation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knowledge_distillation).” You ask a stronger AI model millions of questions. You record its answers, and its reasoning. Then you train your own model to imitate it. It’s like copying a top student’s worked solutions. But you don’t just get the answers. You also learn how they think, for a fraction of the effort.

Chinese labs do this at an enormous scale.

Anthropic says Alibaba alone exchanged [more than 151 million messages](https://www.anthropic.com/threat-intelligence-report-september-2026) with Claude in just three months. The Institute for Progress estimated distillation closes [roughly half the gap](https://ifp.org/how-to-increase-americas-ai-lead-over-china/#how-much-do-chinese-companies-gain-from-adversarial-distillation) between American models and Chinese ones. That’s like giving Chinese AI companies _[four times](https://ifp.org/how-to-increase-americas-ai-lead-over-china/#executive-summary)_ as many chips.

So why don’t American AI companies stop the Chinese ones from copying? To do that, companies have to catch huge numbers of fake accounts. In one campaign, DeepSeek, [Moonshot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moonshot_AI), and [MiniMax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MiniMax_Group) used [roughly 24,000 of them](https://www.anthropic.com/news/detecting-and-preventing-distillation-attacks).

But it _can_ be done. Anthropic says it cut the data that copiers can harvest from its models by [between 90 and 99%](https://www.anthropic.com/news/distillation-defenses).

The catch is that copiers just go wherever the defences are weakest. Zhipu tried to [copy the hacking skills](https://www.anthropic.com/threat-intelligence-report-september-2026) of Anthropic’s top public model, got blocked, but then switched to models with weaker safeguards. Its next model was rated the [most capable hacking model](https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2026/09/caisis-assessment-zais-glm-53-cyber-capabilities) anyone has ever released for free.

And there’s an awkward incentive. Copiers pay to use these models, just like any other customer. So every company that blocks them loses money to the ones that don’t.

### China is running a different race [[00:12:34]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/china-ai-race-chips-slowdown/?t=754)

So China is buying, smuggling, and renting American computing power, and copying American frontier models. Does that mean they’re losing the AI race?

Ask China’s own AI leaders, and they’re surprisingly frank: in the race to build the smartest AI, yes, they’re behind.

[At a conference in Beijing](https://www.chinatalk.media/p/the-all-star-chinese-ai-conversation) in January, [Lin Junyang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Junyang_Lin), who was at that point a technical lead on Alibaba’s Qwen models, put China’s chance of overtaking top American AI companies at [less than 20%](https://interestingengineering.com/ai-robotics/china-us-ai-dominance-race) in the next three to five years. And he called that “highly optimistic.” His reason was computing power.

On the same panel, Zhipu’s chief AI scientist, [Tang Jie](https://keg.cs.tsinghua.edu.cn/jietang/), went further. He said “the gap may in fact be _widening_,” because many of the US’s best models aren’t public.

But building the smartest AI models is only one way to win at AI.

Beijing seems to be running [a different race altogether](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/paul-scharre-ai-warfare-autonomous-weapons/#us-china-balance-of-power-and-surveillance-with-ai-020433): using it everywhere. Its goal isn’t to make the best chatbot. It’s [AI in every factory](https://english.www.gov.cn/policies/latestreleases/202508/27/content_WS68ae7976c6d0868f4e8f51a0.html), hospital, and government office. And in that race, China has real advantages.

For one, it has power. AI data centres need enormous amounts of electricity, and in the US, that’s becoming a real problem. American data centres could face a 44-gigawatt [shortfall by 2028](https://ng.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/morgan-stanley-sees-up-to-20-shortage-of-us-power-for-data-centers-through-2028-2203320). That’s like needing to add another California to the US power grid in just over a year from now.

China does not have that problem. It’s expected to add almost [six times as much generating capacity](https://www.energyconnects.com/news/renewables/2026/february/china-ramps-up-energy-boom-flagged-by-musk-as-key-to-ai-race) as the US over the next five years. So right now, China’s bottleneck is chips. Which means if China ever solves its chip problem, it won’t hit the wall the US is running into. It’ll already have the power to run them.

China also has [factories and robots](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/daniel-kokotajlo-ai-2027-updates-china-robot-economy/#why-we-might-get-a-robot-economy-incredibly-fast-004234). Last year, China installed [about 354,000](https://ifr.org/downloads/press_docs/EN-2026-SEP-24-IFR_Press_Release_WR-CHINA.pdf) industrial robots, which is 59% of the world’s total. The US installed about a tenth as many.

And in the first half of this year, 97% of the humanoid robots sold anywhere in the world were [made by Chinese companies](https://www.eweek.com/news/china-humanoid-robots-agibot-unitree-apac/). It also controls most of the supply chain behind them, from the minerals to the batteries to the powerful magnets that drive robot joints.

So the picture is more complicated than one race with one finish line. In the race the US is running — the one to build the smartest AI — China is still behind. But again, not by that much — which puts the US in a tricky position.

### Why a bigger lead matters [[00:15:30]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/china-ai-race-chips-slowdown/?t=930)

I don’t love the [US–China AI](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/helen-toner-ai-policy-washington-dc/) “race” framing. Treating AI like an arms race is exactly the kind of thinking that pushes everyone to cut corners on safety. But there are a few reasons to want a bigger gap.

For one, it would help the US capture more of AI’s economic gains. And it would let the US shore up its cyber defences before anyone else can attack them.

But the reason I personally care about most is breathing room. I’m extremely worried that we’re building AI faster than we can [make it safe or secure](https://80000hours.org/problem-profiles/artificial-intelligence/). A bigger gap means time to slow down: to test new models properly, and hold back the ones that aren’t ready yet.

And here’s the thing: the US might already have that time. Six months is _actually_ a pretty long time in AI. And because so much of China’s progress comes from distillation — basically copying US models — the real gap is bigger than it looks.

Matt Sheehan, [who studies Chinese AI policy](https://carnegieendowment.org/people/matt-sheehan), compares China to a [wakesurfer riding the wave](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/15/opinion/ezra-klein-podcast-matt-sheehan.html) behind a boat. It keeps up partly because the boat is doing a lot of the work. If the boat slows down, the wave shrinks. China doesn’t _suddenly_ shoot ahead. It would then have to rely on its own engine, which is much smaller.

So the US may already have time to slow down.

### Could the US widen the gap? [[00:16:51]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/china-ai-race-chips-slowdown/?t=1011)

But if it wanted to, how could the US widen the gap even more? Mostly with [powers the government already has](https://ifp.org/how-to-increase-americas-ai-lead-over-china/#how-much-could-policy-interventions-extend-the-us-ai-lead).

First, there’s renting, which lets Chinese companies use huge numbers of American chips abroad. Neither party has stopped it: Biden-era regulators chose not to restrict it, and a later attempt was [scrapped by the Trump administration](https://www.bis.gov/press-release/department-commerce-rescinds-biden-era-artificial-intelligence-diffusion-rule-strengthens-chip-related).

But it’s very fixable. [A bill to help restrict renting](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/BILLS-119hr2683eh/html/BILLS-119hr2683eh.htm) has [already passed the House](https://clerk.house.gov/evs/2026/roll013), so now it just needs to be passed by the Senate.

And regulators don’t even need to wait for the bill. They could _already_ require that [chips sold abroad](https://ifp.org/how-to-increase-americas-ai-lead-over-china/#reducing-china-s-compute-access) can’t be rented out to Chinese companies at scale — ideally alongside a crackdown on smuggling, so the demand doesn’t just go underground.

The government could also stop approving sales of chips like the H200, and limit the gaming cards being used for AI.

And in the long run, the biggest lever might be the older chipmaking machines China still buys from ASML, and the maintenance ASML provides for them. [Some analysts argue](https://techstatecraft.org/duv/) that cutting off both could lock in the US advantage for at least a decade.

Put together, the [Institute for Progress estimates](https://ifp.org/how-to-increase-americas-ai-lead-over-china/#executive-summary) these steps could add several months to the US lead by the end of the year, and maybe even double it. The exact number is rough. But the direction is clear: the size of the lead is in large part a policy choice.

So why hasn’t the US done all this?

Partly, it’s incentives. NVIDIA wants the sales, and copiers are paying customers. But there’s also an argument on the other side — the one [David Sacks](https://news.bloomberglaw.com/ip-law/trump-ai-czar-david-sacks-defends-reversal-of-china-chip-curbs) and [Jensen Huang made](https://www.fortune.com/2025/05/22/NVIDIA-ceo-jensen-huang-failure-us-restrictions-chips-semiconductors-china-ai-artificial-intelligence): cutting China off just pushes it to build its own chips, and reduce its dependence on the US.

Now, Huang runs the company that would lose those sales, so it is tempting to write him off. But researchers with nothing to sell make versions of the same argument.

Analysts at the Center for Strategic and International Studies concluded that [broad US controls have sped up](https://www.csis.org/analysis/chinas-localization-drive-semiconductors-gains-impetus-allied-chip-export-controls) China’s push to stop relying on American technology. So maybe if you cut China off, you give it every reason to build its own technology instead. Once it can, the US would lose that leverage for good.

There’s a second worry too: [controls make cooperation harder](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/luke-muehlhauser-ai-safety-grantmaking-founding/#how-realistic-is-a-deal-with-china-012058). Matt Sheehan says Beijing’s first read of American AI policy is that the US wants to hold China down. That makes any deal between the two countries harder to reach, including one to [slow down together](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/tom-milton-verification-technology-ai-slowdown/#what-would-a-uschina-ai-deal-look-like-005127).

So should the US hold off on closing these gaps? I don’t think so.

China was trying to build its own chips long before the US export controls. Back in 2015, its “[Made in China 2025](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Made_in_China_2025)” plan set a target of [making 70% of its own chips](https://www.csis.org/analysis/chinas-localization-drive-semiconductors-gains-impetus-allied-chip-export-controls).

Selling China chips doesn’t stop it building its own. Remember when the US approved sales of NVIDIA’s H200 this year, Beijing [told its companies to hold off](https://www.rte.ie/news/business/2026/0107/1551989-NVIDIA-china-ai/), _to protect China’s own chip industry._ So Beijing will build its own chips either way. The question is whether it also gets American chips in the meantime.

Then there’s timing. Building a whole chip industry from scratch takes years — maybe even decades. ASML started working on its most advanced machines [in the 1990s](https://www.asml.com/en/news/stories/2022/making-euv-lab-to-fab). They cost billions of dollars and took two decades, and only [entered mass production in 2019](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000937966/000093796620000011/a2019integratedreportb.htm).

If powerful AI is coming in the next five years, as [many experts in the industry believe](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/2026-agi-timelines/), China’s own chips won’t be ready in time. What matters is how close its best models are _now_. And right now, that depends a lot on American chips and American models.

But there’s one more risk, and it could undermine the lead the US already has — even if it does manage to widen the gap.

### What if China just steals the models? [[00:21:12]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/china-ai-race-chips-slowdown/?t=1272)

You might assume the most powerful AI models in the world are [guarded like nuclear secrets](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/sella-nevo-securing-ai-model-weights/#who-tries-to-steal-model-weights-003221).

They are very much not. And that makes two very precious things relatively easy to steal if China wanted to.

One is a model itself. An AI model, at its core, is [one very large file](https://ai-frontiers.org/articles/can-the-us-prevent-agi-from-being-stolen) — so if you steal that file, you’ve [stolen the whole model](https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_briefs/RBA2849-1.html).

The other is how a model was built: [the techniques and breakthroughs](https://situational-awareness.ai/lock-down-the-labs/) that make each new model better than the last.

Security experts rate how well AI companies protect these on a [scale from 1 to 5](https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA2849-1.html). Level 5 means you could stop the world’s most capable spy agencies.

[The best public estimates](https://ai-2027.com/research/security-forecast) put top American AI companies somewhere around a 2 or a 3. [An industry task force](https://sl5.org/) is working out how companies could reach level 5 [by 2028 or 2029](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.08449). But it would be entirely voluntary — nothing would require them to do it.

So a nuclear power plant has to meet [strict federal security rules](https://www.nrc.gov/security.html), but the companies building what might be the most powerful technology in history don’t.

And China is already going after American AI secrets. In January, [Linwei Ding](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/former-google-engineer-found-guilty-economic-espionage-and-theft-confidential-ai-technology), a former Google engineer, was convicted of stealing thousands of pages of Google’s AI secrets while secretly working for two Chinese tech companies. Those pages showed how Google builds the supercomputers it uses to train its AI — which is exactly the kind of computing power China has struggled to build.

No [theft of a top model](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/daniel-kokotajlo-ai-2027-updates-china-robot-economy/#interview-begins-could-china-really-steal-frontier-model-weights-003626) has been publicly confirmed yet. But the techniques behind them are clearly a target.

So how bad would it be if these things were stolen?

I’ll start with the model itself. Once stolen, China gets everything it can do, including the dangerous stuff.

Take hacking. [In August](https://www.wiz.io/blog/php2shell-php-rce), AI models helped researchers find [critical flaws in PHP](https://www.php.net/archive/2026.php#2026-10-21-5), software that runs on [about 70% of the world’s websites](https://w3techs.com/technologies/details/pl-php). The researchers [tried to keep it quiet](https://thephp.foundation/blog/2026/10/21/todays-php-security-release-and-how-were-strengthening-php-security/) while it was fixed. But in October, [details leaked](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cmly0lg3w5x2o), and governments rushed to [pull websites offline](https://www.asiaone.com/digital/php-vulnerabilities-government-websites) before hackers could use them.

If China stole a model like that… they’d basically have a cyberweapon with unprecedented capabilities.

There’s also biology. [Companies already add safeguards](https://www.anthropic.com/news/activating-asl3-protections) because their models might help someone [make a bioweapon](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/richard-moulange-ai-bioweapons-biorisk/). A stolen model comes without those safeguards.

Then there are breakthroughs. A stolen _model_ pretty quickly becomes obsolete. But stolen breakthroughs in how to design or train AI could help China build better models long after they’ve stolen them. That could give China a lasting boost, even with less computing power.

For me, that’s the scariest part, because it could eat into the room the US has to slow down. If the US slows down, China has to make progress on their own, without copying, and with far fewer chips. Stolen breakthroughs could let it close the gap in a lasting way.

But unlike China’s chips, security is entirely in the US’s hands. And [security at American AI companies](https://80000hours.org/career-reviews/ai-security/) could be _much, much_ better than it is right now. It’s honestly kind of crazy that it isn’t better already. But that’s fixable.

### So can the US slow down? [[00:24:53]](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/china-ai-race-chips-slowdown/?t=1493)

China buys, smuggles, and rents American chips. It trains on answers from American models. And with security as weak as it is, China could steal the models themselves, or the techniques behind them.

All of which puts some serious holes in the argument that the US can’t slow down because China will catch up.

So if you care about competing with China, the first step isn’t going faster. It’s to stop giving so much away.

In fact, slowing down might not be as costly as it sounds. A researcher at Forethought estimates that a top American company’s computing edge could let it do research [almost twice as fast](https://newsletter.forethought.org/p/can-the-us-slow-ai-r-and-d-and-keep) as its Chinese counterpart. So the US could put some of that speed into safety and security, and still keep pace.

But a bigger lead only helps if the US actually uses it to make models safer and more secure.

What the US AI companies are doing [right now is terrifying](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/ai-extinction-explained/). They don’t seem to be fully in control of their own models, but they’re [using them to build the next generation of AIs](https://openai.com/index/research-acceleration-view-inside-openai/) anyway.

I’m not certain about all of this. But I am confident of one thing. If the race with China is the reason the US can’t slow down, it should at least be doing the things that would actually keep it ahead.

Because right now, China is renting American chips.

title: The creep fades
content:
The uncanny valley is the place where an image that’s almost human creeps us out:

[![Image 1](https://i0.wp.com/seths.blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/auggie.jpg?resize=769%2C1024&ssl=1)](https://i0.wp.com/seths.blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/auggie.jpg?ssl=1)
Sorry to share that.

Human beings evolved to have a distaste for things that are almost, but not quite, the usual thing. It takes a while for someone who wasn’t raised with cilantro to like it–the same with hot sauce. When Edison first showed people his moving pictures, people screamed. Our brain is warning us that categories are getting surprising and we should be on alert.

As AI spreads through the culture, we’re seeing plenty of mediocre AI-style writing. And then humans subconsciously start writing in that style because they see it so often. And finally, a grudging acceptance that it sounds okay. We’ve been through this a hundred times before.

No one asks to get creeped out. It’s usually done to us, not for us. But, over time, the creep fades.

Like most warnings, we ought to keep two things in mind:

1.   All warnings are not the same. We need to decide which ones to ignore.
2.   Just because a warning fades doesn’t mean that the problem is gone. 

The creepiness fades.

But at the same time, there’s a creeping change as trusted and expected elements of our culture fade away.

title: The Temperamental Nature of Alligator Gender-Reveal Parties
content:
Human embryos grow at a comfortable temperature just a bit warmer than the mother’s body. Reptile embryos, however, are at the whim of outside temperatures. And, in many cases, the sex of the offspring is known to be decided by incubation temperature.

In fact, a [recent study](https://journals.biologists.com/jeb/article-pdf/doi/10.1242/jeb.252972/3722446/jeb252972.pdf) published in the _Journal of Experimental Biology_ found that the sex of American alligators (_Alligator mississippiensis_) is set by just a one- or two-degree difference. With environmental temperatures on the upswing, that could make for lopsided alligator populations.

**Read more: “**[**Animals Are More Rational Than You Think**](https://nautil.us/animals-are-more-rational-than-you-think-1194596)**”**

“Whenever a population is out of balance, it can impact population growth,” explained senior study author Benjamin Parrot, an ecologist at the University of Georgia. “If temperatures are biasing sex ratios, that’s a big issue.”

Researchers collected 145 gator eggs from seven wild gator nests at the Tom Yawkey Wildlife Center in North Carolina. Eggs were incubated in the laboratory under five different temperature conditions: 30°C, 31°C, 32°C, 33°C, or 34°C. Several weeks into their incubation—when sex is known to have been established—embryos were removed from eggs to determine sex based on their reproductive structures.

The development of viable embryos didn’t vary between the temperature treatments, but the sex did. The lowest and highest temperatures favored females, while the medium temperatures favored males. At the higher temperatures, just a degree or two could shift the sex. The results also showed that brief spurts of heat expected to damage the embryos—up to 35.6°C—instead boosted their chances of being female.

With [wild alligator nest temperatures predicted to rise to as hot as 33.5°C by 2100](https://royalsocietypublishing.org/rspb/article/287/1926/20200210/85574/Spatial-and-temporal-variation-in-nest) across their range, expect some truly gender-bending gator trends in the future. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: This 150-Million-Year-Old Bird Had a Body Built for the Land
content:
Lots of birds aren’t built for flight: chickens, penguins, emus, etc. This new species of bird (_Yuezhuornis yangyuanensis_), which lived around 150 million years ago, is another such odd duck (so to speak), though it boasts the added cachet of challenging the conventional understanding of bird evolution.

The traditional view has been that natural selection prioritized characteristics that help birds fly across the millennia. But _Yuezhuornis yangyuanensis_ had a body built more for living on land than in the air. For example, its fossil had sharp teeth, relatively short wings, and a claw on its foot for attacking predators. It’s very much like a small, predatory dinosaur, and experts believe it may not have been able to fly at all.

And yet, it has bird-like features that put it firmly in the Avialae part of the animal kingdom—the evolutionary group where you’ll find modern birds and the extinct relatives closest to them.

The recovered fossil and an image of how Y. yangyuanensis may have looked. _Credit: Min Wang_

“When we examined _Yuezhuornis_, we were struck by its extraordinary mix of features,” Wang Min, one of the authors of [the study](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10972-z) on _Y. yangyuanensis_, explained in a [statement](https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1147488). “It possesses bird-like pelvic and hindlimb structures yet retains the specialized predatory foot and teeth of a small meat-eating dinosaur. It shows us that early bird evolution was far more complicated than we previously realized.”

Either the ancestors of this bird could fly, and this species lost the ability, or the entire lineage was never able to take flight in the first place, indicating that flight evolved more than once in early birds.

The incomplete but well-preserved fossil was recovered in southeastern China and is estimated to have come from a bird about the size of a crow—with a mass of around 1.8 pounds. Its anatomy was compared to other dinosaurs and birds of the same time period, as well as modern species, to see where it might fit on the grand evolutionary timeline. All of the evidence points toward a terrestrial lifestyle in the Late Jurassic.

It was around this epoch that flight evolved for the first time, so the dating matters, but experts still aren’t sure how the ability to fly originated. There are theories that it evolved from predators who launched attacks from elevated positions, or from bipeds who started jumping further and further distances while running, or from animals who ran up steep inclines and used early versions of wings to help.

Whatever the reason, given the carnage and chaos that happened on land during the Late Jurassic, it’s no wonder evolution nudged some creatures into the sky. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Lean Muscle Mass Isn’t a Cure-All for Metabolic Health
content:
You’ve probably heard it your entire adult life—building lean muscle mass is one of the best things you can do for your health. After all, in addition to boosting physical strength and burning calories, lean muscle mass also pulls glucose from the blood and helps protect against diabetes. But now a new study [published](http://dx.doi.org/10.1210/clinem/dgag407) in _The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism_ is challenging that conventional wisdom.

A team of nutritional and chronic disease researchers from Louisiana State University analyzed health data from close to 60,000 adults (between the ages of 37 and 73) enrolled in the U.K. Biobank study. They focused on those who had undergone MRI and low-level X-ray scans capable of determining their fat-free mass, a commonly used proxy for lean muscle mass.

**Read more: “[People With This Neanderthal Hormone Receptor Have More Muscle Mass](https://nautil.us/people-with-this-neanderthal-hormone-receptor-have-more-muscle-mass-1283409)”**

The team then investigated the association between fat-free mass and adverse health outcomes, like developing a metabolic disorder and elevated glycated hemoglobin (for connoisseurs of diabetes pharmaceutical ads, this is the HbA1C they’re always singing about). They also assessed different measures of fat-free mass, like visceral adiposity (abdominal and organ fat) and fat infiltration within muscle tissue.

The results painted a messy picture. For example, higher total fat-free mass (and fat-free mass adjusted for height) was actually associated with a _slightly higher_ likelihood of developing metabolic syndromes and elevated HbA1C. On the other hand, a higher proportion of body weight made up of fat-free mass was associated with a _lower_ likelihood of developing these adverse outcomes.

“The findings suggest that muscle quantity alone may not provide a complete picture of metabolic health and that where fat is stored in the body is an important part of the story,” study author Sri Lakshmi S. Devarakonda said in a [statement](https://www.pbrc.edu/news/media/2026/ukbiobank.aspx).

Drilling down into the data, the team found that visceral fat seemed to have the strongest influence. Those with the same total fat-free mass but more fat around their abdomens and organs were more likely to experience the adverse outcomes. Fatty infiltration into muscle showed the same pattern, albeit slightly weaker.

“Our findings suggest that we need to look beyond the amount of fat-free mass a person has to better understand their metabolic health,” study author Candida Rebello explained. “Where fat is stored in the body matters, particularly fat around internal organs and fat that accumulates within muscle tissue. These different patterns of fat distribution can influence the relationship between fat-free mass and metabolic risk, underscoring the importance of considering the quality and composition of body tissues, not just their quantity, when studying metabolic health.”

Does any of this mean you should avoid building lean muscle mass? Definitely not. It’s still one of the best things you can do for your health. It’s just not a panacea. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Famous Fossil Could be Rosetta Stone for Hidden Hominin Diversity
content:
The discovery of the [Taung child’s skull](https://nautil.us/the-monstrous-raptors-that-threatened-our-ancestors-1286304) in 1924 was a seismic moment in understanding human origins. It was the first _Australopithecus_ specimen ever found. As such, it’s the holotype of the group—the standard measuring stick future specimens were judged by. Now those specimens are coming under renewed scrutiny in a study [published](http://dx.doi.org/10.1038/s44513-026-00008-2) in _npj Palaeoecosystems_.

An international team of paleobiologists decided to give the Taung child’s noggin a fresh look, and the more they looked, the more discrepancies they found. By comparing the rate of tooth mineralization with chimpanzees, gorillas, humans, and other fossils, the team determined the skull likely belonged to a child (not a juvenile as the original investigating anthropologist surmised). Analysis of the dentine-enamel junction (where the tooth’s hard shell meets its chewy center), revealed a resemblance to _Paranthropus robustus_, a more ape-like hominin that likely originated after _Australopithecus_.

**Read more: “**[**What Made Early Humans Smart**](https://nautil.us/what-made-early-humans-smart-238238)**”**

Focusing on the braincase, the researchers found other discrepancies. Using chimp and gorilla skull growth as a guide, they compared digitally reconstructed skulls found in the same region and purported to belong to _Australopithecus_ to the Taung child’s braincase. They found that the size and shape of the Taung child’s skull indicate it could have grown into a hominin resembling some of the _Australopithecus_ specimens, but not others.

In other words, the team’s modeling indicates there was a lot more variation among hominins living in the area at the time, and lumping them all into _Australopithecus_ may downplay this diversity. Their investigation of the paleoclimate at the time paints a picture of a region in flux, and they hypothesize these shifts were fueling hominin diversity. As wet and dry cycles continually remodeled the region, hominin populations expanded and contracted, confronting new pathogens and predators, diverging, and interbreeding, according to their theory.

“For over 100 years, we assumed the Taung Child was just one of many similar fossils from the era,” study author Gabriele Macho of Vrije Universiteit Brussel said in a statement. “Our findings turn that on its head. The human family tree wasn’t a neat, straight trunk—it was a chaotic, tangled bush driven by climate shifts.”

Of course, it’s important to note it’s merely a hypothesis. Still, if the past 20 years have taught us anything, it’s that our family tree has [more branches](https://nautil.us/youre-carrying-ghost-dna-from-extinct-hominins-1283291) than we previously thought.![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Researchers Can Tell How Lonely You Are by Your Instagram Activity
content:
Meta is about to make some [hefty payouts](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/meta-reaches-17-billion-settlement-with-states-in-landmark-trial-over-teen-social-media-addiction) to state governments—over $17 billion in total. The parent company of Facebook and Instagram recently settled a lawsuit (brought by nearly every state’s attorney general) alleging their platforms don’t do nearly enough to prevent teen social media addiction. As part of the settlement, the company is promising to do more to prevent their products from harming children. Now, a new study [published](https://www.nature.com/articles/s44184-026-00252-z) in _npj Mental Health Research_ is showing a potential path forward.

A team of psychologists from University of California San Diego convinced 415 undergraduate students to give them access to the data from their Instagram accounts, including all of their photographs, captions, likes, and comments they’d ever posted. Most previous studies have relied solely on publicly available data, so getting access to private accounts—which more than 60 percent of the students used—gave the researchers a more comprehensive look at everyday behaviors. The students also completed questionnaires designed to measure their feelings of loneliness.

**Read more: “**[**This Giant Waterlily Species Was Discovered Via Instagram**](https://nautil.us/this-giant-waterlily-species-was-discovered-via-instagram-1285947)**”**

The team then used machine learning to parse the data and identify patterns, comparing the students’ activity to their self-reported loneliness measures. “What’s remarkable is that we can identify patterns associated with something as personal and difficult to observe as loneliness,” study author Sherry (Yueyi) Jiang said in a [statement](https://today.ucsd.edu/story/your-instagram-can-predict-how-lonely-you-are). “By looking at photos, language, and everyday activity together, we can pick up on subtle clues that might otherwise go unnoticed.”

So what are these subtle clues?

According to the team, those who reported feeling lonely were more likely to use a profile photo featuring an upward head tilt, less likely to post photos with faces, and tended to use past-tense language in captions (like “was” and “had”).

Of course, not all loneliness is the same. The researchers distinguished between the students who experienced emotional loneliness, or the lack of meaningful connections, and social loneliness, the feeling of being disconnected from a community of friends or family.

Behavioral, visual, and linguistic clues to loneliness in Instagram activity. _Credit: University of California San Diego_

While both groups shared the aforementioned hallmarks of general lonely posting, the emotionally lonely had profile pics expressing sadness or anger, tended to post more at night, used more negative language, but also referenced friends or family more often. The socially lonely were stingier with their likes and comments, posted less often on weekends, and used fewer words expressing appreciation (like “thank” and “care”).

The team says because someone’s posting behaviors seem to offer insights into their emotional state, it could provide an opportunity for social media platforms to intervene. For example, late-night negative posting could trigger a message prompting users to reach out and seek help. Better understanding the dimensions of loneliness could tailor these suggestions to individual users’ experiences.

“Loneliness isn’t a one-size-fits-all experience, and neither are the solutions,” study author Piotr Winkielman explained. “Someone who feels disconnected from a broader community may benefit from more opportunities to socialize, while someone who lacks a close emotional connection may need a very different kind of support.”

Whether any changes get implemented—and whether they’re effective—remains to be seen. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Descendants of Chornobyl’s Pets Run Wild
content:
It’s been more than [40 years since the core meltdown of the Chornobyl nuclear reactor](https://nautil.us/chernobyl-40-years-later-1280322) in what’s now Ukraine. Yet, its ramifications are still visible—not only in [health problems for humans exposed to the radiation](https://carnegieendowment.org/emissary/2026/04/chernobyl-anniversary-nuclear-power-lessons), but also in animal populations.

When people were evacuated from the Chornobyl Exclusion Zone (CEZ) in 1986, many had to leave their dogs behind. Later, efforts were made to eradicate what had become a wild population of radiation-exposed dogs, but some escaped detection. As such, several hundred dogs now roam the CEZ, offering a look at more than 30 generations of genomic response to radiation exposure and associated contamination.

**Read more:**[**“Chernobyl, 40 Years Later”**](https://nautil.us/chernobyl-40-years-later-1280322)

A [study from 2023](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.ade2537) found that these dogs were genetically different from those living 10 miles away in Chornobyl City, and a [recent study](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4425/17/10/1195) published in the journal _Genes_ delved deeper into the causes. “Are the genetic differences due to selection, or are they due to genetic drift over time in an isolated population?” asked lead author Megan Dillon, a veterinary researcher at North Carolina State University.

If the changes are from genetic drift, they should be random, with no relation to adaptations to the environment. If they’re from natural selection, they should favor genes for certain traits—in what’s called directional selection, for example in response to environmental stressors around Chornobyl. The CEZ is contaminated not only with radioactivity, but also with metals, organic compounds, pesticides, and asbestos.

Dillon and her coauthors compared the exposed dog population to three other unexposed feral dog populations in Chornobyl City, Eastern Europe, and the Galápagos Islands. The radiation-exposed dogs stood out genetically from all the others. In fact, the Chornobyl City dogs were actually more like canines in faraway Galápagos than those just 10 miles away in the CEZ.

An analysis of the CEZ genomes found evidence of directional selection in more than 100 genes. While there’s no way to be sure that the genetic changes weren’t from random drift, the results certainly point to adaptation. “When we dig deeper into those genomic regions, we find that these genes are involved in biologically relevant pathways that could allow them to overcome the effects of being exposed to toxicants in this environment,” added Dillon.

And so, despite the attempts to eliminate the pet dogs left behind in the CEZ, they’ve not only survived their new habitat but adapted to it as well. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: The Difference Between Nice and Kind
content:
Perhaps you have heard the [story](https://www.auschwitz.org/en/education/e-learning/podcast/the-sacrifice-and-death-of-father-maximilian-kolbe/) of the Polish Franciscan friar who volunteered to die in place of a total stranger at the Auschwitz concentration camp in 1941. When Nazi guards selected ten prisoners to starve to death in retaliation for an escape, one of those men, Franciszek Gajowniczek, cried out for his family. The friar, Maximilian Kolbe, stepped forward to take his place.

It is hard to imagine a more selfless act. But the concept of selflessness has long been the subject of intense debate among theologians, economists, philosophers, and biologists. English philosopher Thomas Hobbes famously argued that every human action is ultimately driven by pure self-interest: If you help someone at a cost to yourself, you do it because it relieves your own empathic distress or puffs you up with pride.

**Read more: “**[**How Discovering an Equation for Altruism Cost George Price Everything**](https://nautil.us/how-discovering-an-equation-for-altruism-cost-george-price-everything-236658)**”**

For biologists like Richard Dawkins, altruism toward one’s kin or tribe is an evolutionary imperative: It helps to ensure the survival of the group, the species or some twist of shared DNA. More recently, neuroscientists have found that altruism [stimulates](https://www.pnas.org/doi/abs/10.1073/pnas.0604475103) the same regions of the brain that are triggered by pleasurable experiences like eating chocolate or winning a game.

One question at the core of the debate over the nature of altruism pertains to how it is perceived by others, including the recipients of the good deed and the broader public. Professor of clinical psychology Jennifer Cheavens of Ohio State University, who teaches a positive psychology class to undergraduates, recently took inspiration from her students to investigate this question. Cheavens’ students argued that there is a distinction between acts that are _kind_ and acts that are _nice_. Nice is doing a good deed out of obligation or to win reputation points, and is not perceived favorably by others, they held. Kind is doing something without the expectation of any transactional reward, and is perceived more generously.

But what Cheavens found in the lab was the opposite.

Cheavens teamed up with her colleague Laura Wagner, a developmental psychology professor and linguist at Ohio State University. Together they recruited 736 mostly white participants from the United States to read and rate vignettes describing prosocial behavior—described as any action that benefits individuals or society as a whole. What they discovered was that prosocial behavior was almost universally considered a positive thing among their participants: “At least kind, maybe also nice and possibly even caring,” Cheavens said in a [statement](https://news.osu.edu/nice-by-any-other-name--means-essentially-the-same-thing/). Acts that were planned in advance, performed with warmth, and delivered without expectation or obligation were seen as warmer, kinder, and more caring.

For their [study](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s41042-026-00334-5), Wagner and Cheavens along with a team of scientists wrote 14 short stories that contained variations on several dimensions of altruism: anonymity, benefit, cost, expectation, planning, warmth, and relationship to the recipient. Each of the study participants read seven of the stories and was asked to put themselves in the shoes of the recipient of different acts of kindness: Things as simple as someone holding a door, paying for a snack, or donating $500 anonymously. The participants rated each act in terms of how “kind,” how “nice,” and how “caring,” it was.

Modeling the results suggested few differences in perceptions of “kind” and “nice” acts, but the participants had a higher threshold for labeling behaviors as “caring.” Good deeds aimed at someone the do-gooder knew personally were perceived as more caring, as were acts that were more costly to the giver. Kindness, the researchers concluded, may be the term “least likely to be linked to barriers to engaging in prosocial behaviors,” while caring was associated with the highest thresholds. Cheavens and her colleagues suggest the findings could have implications for the kind of language used by prosocial programs that aim to recruit the public. Perhaps encouraging people to be “kind” rather than “caring” will result in more uptake and volunteerism.

So does selflessness exist?

That’s a debate science and philosophy still haven’t settled. But in the meantime, good deeds and acts of kindness are what hold communities together. We need acts of kindness, niceness, and caring to keep happening , whether we’re givers or receivers, and no matter how we refer to them. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: How a Metabolic Spark Could Have Jump-Started Life
content:
## How a Metabolic Spark Could Have Jump-Started Life

Energetic pathways that make and break complex molecules are critical to all life. It’s even possible that these self-sustaining cycles could have been key to life’s beginning.

_This explainer is part of_ Quanta Magazine _’s_ _[Origins of Life Week](https://www.quantamagazine.org/tag/origins-of-life-week/)_ _. Check back throughout the week for more stories about one of science’s biggest unknowns._

F or well over 4 billion years, the fire of metabolism has powered the engines of life. The ability of cells to gather, transform, and harness chemical energy from their surroundings is the central force driving the dizzyingly complex network of chemical reactions that sustains living things.

Metabolism is so crucial to life that some researchers believe that these reactions could have helped spark life itself. They argue that life’s first glimmers were found in self-sustaining cycles of simple molecules, before genes or cells existed. Only later did more complex molecules like RNA and DNA develop and begin storing information for the purposes of heredity.

The core argument behind metabolism’s primacy is that without a self-sustaining reaction to provide energy, it’s impossible to explain how the larger and more complex molecules necessary for cellular life could have been produced at all. Energy going through the system is what life is in its many manifestations, said [William Martin (opens a new tab)](https://www.molevol.hhu.de/en/wfm), an evolutionary biologist at Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf in Germany. “It synthesizes genes that contain the information to produce the catalysts that keep this reaction going, and those catalysts have changed over time.”

The concept that reactions driven by nonliving geochemistry could have eventually triggered living biochemistry has been decades in the making. In 1968, the American biophysicist [Harold Morowitz (opens a new tab)](https://news.yale.edu/2016/03/29/memoriam-harold-j-morowitz-expert-origin-life) proposed that energy that flows through a system organizes that system, and he applied this to the concept of a proto-metabolism. Essentially, Morowitz suggested that energy from external environmental sources, such as the sun or geologic processes, could nudge chemical networks into self-sustaining reactions because they were thermodynamically favored. In time, those could become biological reactions.

A very simple version of early self-sustaining reactions might be something like the acetyl-CoA pathway, a process that some modern microbes use to build complex organic molecules and generate chemical energy from hydrogen and carbon dioxide. But what conditions could have sparked these types of lifelike reactions?

Deep-sea submersibles first encountered hydrothermal vents in the late 1970s. These are wounds in the seafloor where geothermally heated water rich in dissolved metals pours out into the surrounding seawater. In the late 1980s and early 1990s, Günter Wächtershäuser, a patent lawyer with a doctorate in chemistry,[proposed the concept (opens a new tab)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01808279) of an “iron-sulfur world.” In this possible early Earth environment, self-sustaining reactions like the acetyl-CoA pathway could have been chemically catalyzed by the iron-sulfide minerals collecting around these vents.

Here’s how that could have led to life. At first, a very simple pathway might have converted carbon dioxide and hydrogen into more complex carbon-containing compounds such as acetate and pyruvate, and released energy back into the environment. Hydrogen would have provided the energy; metallic catalysts kept this running in a loop. Once a primitive cycle was established, it could begin to produce increasingly complex compounds in layers, with more and more enzymatic loops, all gathering and releasing energy, building out from this original cycle. It’s possible that they could continue increasing in complexity well before any of life’s genetic mechanisms of inheritance had developed.

“You start out with a simple inorganic catalyst, and then organic catalysts, and then enzymes, and the metabolic process becomes more complex,” Martin said. “But the nature of the reactions that start without enzymes has been up in the air and hotly debated.”

To explore possible mechanisms, Martin and his colleagues mimicked temperature and pressure conditions around hydrothermal vents in the laboratory. In 2020, the team showed that chemicals found in these vents, such as carbon dioxide and hydrogen, along with nickel and iron minerals common at these sites, could combine to [create formate, acetate, and pyruvate (opens a new tab)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41559-020-1125-6). These compounds are essentially the “spine” of the acetyl-CoA pathway, said [Martina Preiner (opens a new tab)](https://www.mpi-marburg.mpg.de/martina-preiner), a biochemist at the Max Planck Institute for Terrestrial Microbiology in Germany and lead author of the study. The findings “show that it’s possible to start these reactions before you have anything else,” including RNA or proteins, Preiner said.

However, some scientists argue that the heated and pressurized conditions around hydrothermal vents may not have been required to form these reactions. Also in 2020, [Ramanarayanan Krishnamurthy (opens a new tab)](https://www.scripps.edu/faculty/krishnamurthy/), an organic chemist at Scripps Research in California, and his colleagues demonstrated that two small molecules that may have been present in an early Earth environment, pyruvate and glyoxylate, could react to form almost all the components of the reverse citric acid cycle — which is analogous to the acetyl-CoA cycle — and could do so not only at temperatures and in water conditions far removed from the more extreme environment of a vent, but also without any metal catalysts. This suggests that metabolism could have kicked off in a tepid pool rather than a deep-sea crucible.

Whatever environment provided the trigger, there is no well-formed understanding of how initial metabolic reactions could have become stable enough to develop complexity. Genetic material that can store and replicate information may have been necessary to transmit improvements to rudimentary metabolic reactions across generations.

Researchers also need to establish a connection between metabolism and genetic information, as well as determine how these proto-metabolic reactions might have coexisted without sabotaging each other once they were placed within the confines of cell membranes.

“How best can we mix them together so that we don’t get a complete mess that we can’t analyze?” Krishnamurthy said. “That is the challenge.”
